இறு வரை புரையுமாறு இரு கரை ஏமத்து,
வரை புரை உருவின் நுரை பல சுமந்து,
கை வளை, ஆழி, தொய்யகம், புனை துகில்,
reading: On every side the town cries out: the flood has spread over the lilies of the pond, it has wrecked the dolls the young women drew in the sand and they weep, it has reached the cut sheaves of young paddy so the drum is beaten, the tide has ringed the town, the sky has lost its sluices; it has taken the singers' hamlet and the dancers' street, run into the fields, let the carp eat the spathes, raised the seed-beds into mounds; it rushes like the swell of desire, the field-workers with the shoaling carp spread the water, the banks are guarded like hills, it bears hill-like foam, roofs itself with flowers and spreads through the groves; and as the bathers deck their ears and pluck their garlands, it carries off bangles, rings, armlets, cloth and girdles, entering like the Pandya into the land of his enemies: such is the beauty of the Vaiyai of the king whose army killed his foes.
nuance: The list of cries (lines 23 to 35) is the flood seen by those it harms, and the poet keeps it in praise: losses of sand dolls and seed-beds are counted as the river's wealth. The closing simile turns the river's taking of the bathers' jewels into the Pandya's plunder of enemy country, so the river's beauty (வனப்பு, line 50) is put in the king's possession. Lines 36 and 37 (the swell of desire that joins women who will not understand when told) are hard to construe; the flood's speed seems compared to the haste of passion.

thinai_evidence.note: the river's flood and its spoils told as praise of the Pandya's Vaiyai: paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the flood seizing the bathers' ornaments

tamil: துரந்து புனல் தூவ, தூ மலர்க் கண்கள்
ஏக்கழுத்து நாணான் கரும்பின் அணை மென் தோள்
போக்கிச் சிறைப்பிடித்தாள்; ஓர் பொன் அம் கொம்பு
பரிந்து அவளைக் கைப் பிணை நீக்குவான் பாய்வாள்;
இரும்பு ஈர் வடி ஒத்து மை விளங்கும் கண் ஒளியால்
சுரும்பு ஆர்க்கும் சூர் நறா ஏந்தினாள் கண் நெய்தல்;
பேர் மகிழ் செய்யும் பெரு நறாப் பேணியவே,
கண் இயல் கண்டு ஏத்தி, காரிகை நீர் நோக்கினைப்
பாண் ஆதரித்துப் பல பாட; அப் பாட்டுப்
சிகை கிடந்த ஊடலின் செங் கண் சேப்பு ஊர,
பகை தொடர்ந்து, கோதை பரியூஉ, நனி வெகுண்டு,
யாறு ஆடு மேனி அணி கண்ட தன் அன்பன்
சேறு ஆடு மேனி திருநிலத்து உய்ப்ப, சிரம் மிதித்து,
reading: Among the bathers the water is flung till flower-like eyes redden; one woman, unashamed and proud, takes a man captive in her soft shoulders, and a gold-creeper of a girl leaps to free him from her grip, and the light of their kohl eyes, like a keen iron blade, darkens the red new flood; another, to dry her wet ornaments, lifts bee-humming toddy, and her neythal eyes turn to the strong drink; then a bard, seeing a woman's eyes, sings many songs in praise of her watery glance, and one woman, hating the song, is overcome, the broad-chested lover trembles at what will come to him, and she, eyes red with oodal, quarrels among the women, tears her garland, and in a fury brings down her man, who had looked at the ornaments of the bathing bodies, into the mud and treads on his head, fighting without end while the whole town bathes in the red flood.
nuance: The song moves from the river's beauty to a lovers' quarrel without leaving the flood: the oodal of lines 67 to 76 is caused by the bard's praise of another woman's eyes and by the man's looking (யாறு ஆடு மேனி அணி கண்ட, line 73), and it is told as a public scene, the town going on with its bathing around it. The trembling lover (என்னை வருவது எனக்கு?, line 68) is comic, and the head trodden in the mud is the akam sulk acted out in full. No colophon names a speaker; the poet narrates, so there is no thurai_akam.

thinai_evidence.note: a jealous sulk at a river bathing, the marutham situation of oodal

comparisons.tenor: the girl who rushes to free the man
the eyes of the woman holding toddy

tamil: புரி நரம்பு இன் கொளைப் புகல் பாலை ஏழும்
குழல் அளந்து நிற்ப; முழவு எழுந்து ஆர்ப்ப;
தாமம் தலை புனை பேஎம் நீர் வையை!
reading: The seven paalai modes on the twisted strings, the lute and the voice join, the flute keeps the measure, the drum rises and roars, and the women of the king's house and the singers begin to dance; the beauty of the water that pours down fighting its banks is like the roar where thunder strikes; and the poet hails the Vaiyai of the bewildering water, whose bathers at the ford of Tirumarutham wear garlands on their heads: singing your bounty till dawn we are safe, and pray that we may bathe in you and never leave it, now that we have joined.
nuance: The music of lines 77 to 80 is the festival's, and the poem's own pan is பாலையாழ், so the song names its mode inside itself (பாலை ஏழும், line 77). Line 85 has a gap; the closing prayer asks for the bathing never to end (நீங்காமை, line 86), the same wish akam lovers make of each other, here made of the river.

thinai_evidence.note: the closing address and prayer to the river: paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the roar of the water pouring down

title: செவ்வேள் (8)
theme: Paripadal 8, to Sevvel at Parankundram: the thirty-three gods take refuge in him and the hill equals the Himalaya of his birth; the rains, creatures and flowers make his procession to Koodal; the hill's fame is unending love; a wife forbids her guilty husband to swear by Murugan and turns her grief to worship; the festival crowd's offerings and petitions; bathing lovers at the pool, and a prayer that the hill's waters outlast the rain.
source_issues: Paripadal 8: the colophon has no thinai or thurai; the pan பாலையாழ் is a musical mode, not a thinai.
Paripadal 8 line 9 and line 52 have gaps (dots in the source), and line 1 has dashes after மண்மிசை (flags).
Paripadal 8 line 51: flagged as a line once taken for a modern heading; it reads as verse and the units count it (flag).
Paripadal 8 lines 23, 24, 48, 49, 73 and 74 are not in sangamtamil.com's text; ours kept (flags).
Paripadal 8 line 117: lost vowel sign ொ restored in the -ஒடு fault (flag).
Paripadal 8 line 119: மாரண் is likely a misprint for மாரன்.
Paripadal 8 lines 85-89 are obscure in sense and speaker as the text stands.

tamil: மருந்து உரை இருவரும், திருந்து நூல் எண்மரும்,
reading: The poet lists the gods who have come to cling to Murugan as their refuge: Thirumal of the bird banner and blooming tulasi, the rider of the bull, the first one on the lotus, the twelve who drive darkness from the world, the two who speak of medicine, the eight of the ordered texts, the eleven lords named from the lord of Aathirai, the guardians of the quarters, gods, asuras and the great ascetics; because of him Parankundram equals the Himalaya, and the pool of his hill, where falls hang like garlands, equals the one still pool of the Himalaya where the ranked lotus that bore him blooms in flashing clusters.
nuance: Lines 4 to 7 count the Vedic thirty-three by their groups (10 and 2, 2, 8, 11), so the hill is made the meeting place of the whole older pantheon. The argument of lines 11 to 16 is a transfer of sanctity: the Pandya hill equals the Himalaya because its pool equals the pool of his birth. மாலைச் சுனை (line 16) can be the garland-like pool of the falls or the pool at evening.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god through the gods who serve him and the hill that equals his birthplace, under paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the falls hanging into the pool

tamil: குரல் கேட்ட கோழி குன்று அதிரக் கூவ,
ஏழ் புழை ஐம் புழை யாழ் இசை கேழ்த்து அன்ன, இனம்
வீழ் தும்பி வண்டொடு மிஞிறு ஆர்ப்ப, சுனை மலர,
கொன்றை கொடி இணர் ஊழ்ப்ப, கொடி மலர்
மன்றல மலர, மலர் காந்தள் வாய் நாற,
நன்று அவிழ் பல் மலர் நாற, நறை பனிப்ப,
reading: The rain cloud's voice answers like one that has heard the trumpeting of the god's elephant; hearing it the cocks crow till the hill shakes, the musth elephants trumpet back and the caves return the echo; bees of every kind hum like the music of seven-holed and five-holed instruments, the pools bloom, the konrai lets down its clusters, the creepers flower for weddings, the kanthal opens its mouth, honey drips and the south breeze stirs, and this, the poet says, is the splendour of the coming from your hill to Koodal.
nuance: The unit is a chain of answering sounds (elephant, cloud, cock, elephant, cave) that turns into a chain of opening flowers; the god's presence is heard before it is seen. கூடல் வரவு (line 28) makes the scene a procession from the hill to the Pandya city, not only a landscape.

thinai_evidence.note: the season and the hill's creatures praised as the god's own procession, under paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the thunder of the rain cloud

comparisons.vehicle: ஏழ் புழை ஐம் புழை யாழ் இசை
comparisons.tenor: the hum of the swarming bees

tamil: மன்றல் கலந்த மணி முரசின் ஆர்ப்பு எழ,
வடு வகிர் வென்ற கண், மாந் தளிர் மேனி,
நெடு மென் பணைத் தோள், குறுந் தொடி, மகளிர்
reading: Hailing the god whose shining spear split the mountain, the poet says that when the wedding drums of Koodal roar, the hill answers back and forth like the wind-churned sea, like the cloud drinking the ocean, like Indra's thunder, and its answer is a proclamation: the humming of the bee swarms, the lovers' messengers, rings over the walls of their old town; women with eyes finer than cut mango, bodies like mango shoots, bamboo shoulders and small bangles find on the grove beds of the hill a desire that is never sated, an enjoyment that does not end, a love never complete, and the young men's union, unparting like the makanril pair on spread flowers, is a joy that never fades; such is the fame of cool Parankundram, which gives without forgetting.
nuance: The hill's fame is stated as erotic, not ascetic: the god's hill is praised as the place where love never reaches its end (ஆராக் காமம், வரையா நுகர்ச்சி, முடியா நுகர்ச்சி, முற்றாக் காதல்), a string of negated limits that matches the praise of the god's own boundlessness. The makanril, the water bird proverbial for never leaving its mate, is here part of a comparison of the young men's union, not a separate carrier, so it is not iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill praised by the love it grants: paadaan carrying akam matter

comparisons.tenor: the young men's union with the women

tamil: மாலைக்கு மாலை வரூஉம்; வரை சூள் நில்--
கனியின் மலரின் மலிர் கால் சீப்பு இன்னது;
‘என் பாணி நில் நில்---எலாஅ!--பாணி நீ, நின் சூள்;
"இருள் மை ஈர் உண் கண் இலங்கு இழை ஈன்றாட்கு
வரு புனல் வையை மணல் தொட்டேன்; தரு மண வேள்
ஏழ் உலகும் ஆளி திரு வரைவேல் அன்பு அளிதோ?
என்னை அருளி அருள் முருகு சூள் சூளின்,
நின்னை அருள் இல் அணங்கான் மெய் வேல் தின்னும்;
விறல் வெய்யோன் ஊர் மயில், வேல் நிழல், நோக்கி;
அறவர் அடி தொடினும், ஆங்கு அவை சூளேல்;
குறவன் மகள் ஆணை கூறு ஏலா! கூறேல்;
வையைக்குத் தக்க மணல் சீர் சூள் கூறல்!‘
reading: A wife accuses her husband: he smells of strangers, has played on the hill with dewy-eyed women and comes back smiling evening after evening, gone at morning and home at night, so let him stop swearing by the hill; he answers that the scent is only the wind off the Vaigai groves and the dewy slopes, and begs her not to sulk; she cuts him off, calls him the unworthy son of worthy parents, mimics the oath he will offer (I touched the Vaigai's sand, I touched the foot of the hill of the god who grants marriage), and forbids him to swear by Murugan, by the peacock and the shadow of the spear, by the feet of holy men or by the hunter's daughter, since the true spear of that god would devour him; if he must swear, let him swear by the hill and the sand of the Vaigai.
nuance: Her refusal is protective as much as scornful: she does not doubt that the god enforces an oath (அணங்கான் மெய் வேல் தின்னும், line 66), she doubts the man, and so she steers him to an oath by sand, which cannot strike him. குறவன் மகள் (line 69) is Valli, already a name to swear by. The speaker of lines 51 to 55 is not marked, and the turns between wife and husband are a reading.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife's sulking at a husband who smells of other women and offers oaths: the oodal of marutham

tamil: யார் பிரிய, யார் வர, யார் வினவ, யார் செப்பு?
‘நீர் உரைசெய் நீர்மை இல் சூள் என்றி,‘ நேரிழாய்!
கய வாய் நெய்தல் அலர், கமழ்முகை மண நகை
நயவரு நறவு இதழ், மதர் உண்கண்; வாள் நுதல்;
முகை முல்லை வென்று, எழில் முத்து ஏய்க்கும் வெண் பல்
நகை சான்ற கனவு அன்று; நனவு அன்று நவின்றதை:
இடு துனி கை ஆறா என், துயர் கூரச்
சுடும், இறை; ஆற்றிசின், அடி சேர்ந்து! சாற்றுமின்
‘தெரி இழாய் செல்க!‘ என்றாய்; எல்லா! யாம் பெற்றேம்,
ஒருவர்க்கும் பொய்யா நின் வாய் இல் சூள் வௌவல்;
பருவத்துப் பல் மாண் நீ சேறவின் காண்டை
செருவம் செயற்கு என்னை முன்னை, தன் சென்னி,
reading: The quarrel goes on (who left, who came, who asked, who told?): he says she calls his oath worthless and praises her neythal eyes, bud-like smile, honeyed lips, bright brow and teeth whiter than jasmine buds and like pearls, saying what he speaks is neither dream nor waking; she says the anger she has taken on will not cool and her grief grows, and turns to the god: let us go to his feet, offer flowers, feed the fire with oblation and beat the rhythm at cool Parankundram, where Murugan of the drum is worshipped; then she mocks the oath again, saying she has caught the oath from his mouth that never lies to anyone, and the unit ends in obscure lines about a bull, a goad and the hanging bell struck by hand.
nuance: The love quarrel turns into a vow of worship in the middle of a sentence (lines 78 to 82): the god at the hill is the one place where the wife's grief can be taken. ஒருவர்க்கும் பொய்யா நின் வாய் (line 84) is sarcasm. Lines 85 to 89 (எருமை இருத் தோட்டி, காளை, தூங்கு மணி) are not secure in sense or speaker.

thinai_evidence.note: the same husband-and-wife quarrel over the oath, now turned to the god

tamil: நாறு கமழ் வீயும், கூறும் இசை முழவமும்,
நனவின் சேஎப்ப நின் நளி புனல் வையை
பாடுவார் பாணிச் சீரும், ஆடுவார் அரங்கத் தாளமும்,
reading: From the wind-beaten peaks the rain swells, the branches drip, the groves bloom, the pools fill with mud and the broad road is spread with marutham sand and flowers, and the small-footed women rise to join the festival; the worshippers carry sandal of many kinds, incense, lamps the wind cannot put out, fragrant flowers, drums, bells, ropes, peacocks, axes and the elephant image, and they ask their boons: some that what their hand touched in a dream should come true in waking, and that the Vaigai's flood adorn them, some vow that a child come to the womb, some whisper that their work for wealth succeed, some worship that their lord win in battle; the songs' rhythms, the dancers' beats on the stage and the thunder of the cloud-swept hill make a clamour that never sleeps.
nuance: The petitions are this-worldly and specific (a lover seen in a dream, a child, wealth from work, a husband's victory), and each is matched to a ritual act: asking a boon, making a vow, speaking into the god's ear, offering worship. அரு வரைச் சேராத் தொழுநர் (line 102) may be worshippers who do not climb the hill and pray from its foot.

thinai_evidence.note: the festival crowd's offerings and petitions to the god, under paadaan

tamil: ஆய் இதழ் உண்கண் அலர் முகத் தாமரை,
எம் கைப் பதுமம், கொங்கைக் கய முகை,
செவ் வாய் ஆம்பல் செல் நீர்த் தாமரை,
கடம்பு அமர் செல்வன் கடி நகர் பேண
நெறி நீர் அருவி அசும்பு உறு செல்வம்,
reading: Girls rise after diving in the green pool, and their eyes, open faces, feet, golden ear ornaments, hands, budding breasts and red mouths are so like the lotus, water lily and the other flowers of the flowing water that the two cannot be told apart; the sharp-toothed women's breast ornaments meet the chests of men handsome as the god of love, the men give the women the nectar of joy as their right, and the women with bodies like red shoots ease the young men's longing; so lovers bound in marriage and those not yet together gather to honour the guarded town of the lord who dwells in the kadambu, and the poet prays that the wealth of streaming falls and springs, the gift of the god born to the dark-throated lord from the spotless lady, may last for cool Parankundram even when the sky dries up and the earth cracks.
nuance: The bathing girls become the pool's flowers (புலம் வேறுபாடுறா, line 117), so the shrine's water is where love and worship join, and the closing prayer asks that this water, not the rain, be permanent. எம் கைப் பதுமம் (line 115) slips into a first-person voice. Lines 127 and 128 (மறு மிடற்று அண்ணற்கு மாசிலோள் தந்த) are read here as naming the god as the son Uma gave to Siva; they could also make the falls her gift.

words: கடம்பு அமர் செல்வன் கடி நகர் பேண
thinai_evidence.note: lovers' play at the pool ending in worship and a prayer for the hill: paadaan carrying akam matter

title: செவ்வேள் (9)
theme: Paripadal 9, to Sevvel at Parankunram: his birth from Siva and his wedding to Indra's daughter on the hill, a lesson to Vedic scholars in the Tamil order of love and the sulk, the quarrel of his two wives and their women's mock battle, contests of the performers, and closing praise of the lord of both karpu and love.
source_issues: Paripadal 9: the colophon has no thinai or thurai; the pan is பாலையாழ், a musical mode, not a thinai.
Paripadal 9 lines 15 and 29 are not in sangamtamil.com's text; ours kept (flags).
Paripadal 9 line 79: repaired from sangamtamil.com's reading (encoding junk or a lost first letter); the sense of மேஎ எஃகினவை is thin.
Paripadal 9 lines 3, 49 and 58: words run together without a space (சிமைஉயர்ந்தவர், நுசுப்பார்நூழில், அகலத்தவனைவானவன்).
Paripadal 9 lines 18-22: சுணங்கறை is a rare word and the passage may be corrupt; read with caution.

tamil: இரு நிலம் துளங்காமை வடவயின் நிவந்து ஓங்கி,
அரு நிலை உயர் தெய்வத்து அணங்குசால் தலை காக்கும்,
எரி மலர்த் தாமரை இறை வீழ்த்த பெரு வாரி
விரி சடைப் பொறை ஊழ்த்து, விழு நிகர் மலர் ஏய்ப்ப,
மணி மிடற்று அண்ணற்கு, மதி ஆரல் பிறந்தோய்! நீ.
மை இரு நூற்று இமை உண்கண் மான் மறி தோள் மணந்த ஞான்று,
ஐ-இருநூற்று மெய்ந் நயனத்தவன் மகள் மலர் உண்கண்,
மணி மழை தலைஇயென, மா வேனில் கார் ஏற்று,
reading: The poet hails Murugan as born of the blue-throated lord who, when the high gods of the northern mountain agreed, took on his spread matted hair the great flood that the lord of the lotus let fall and held it lightly like a flower, and says that on the day the god married the doe-eyed daughter of the thousand-eyed Indra her flower eyes rained like drops of gems, and his own Parankunram took in the dark rain in the heart of summer and the cool rain did not stop.
nuance: The wedding is marked by rain out of season: the bride's eyes raining and the hill's summer rain are set side by side, so the hill is made a sacred place by an event, not by nature. Indra's thousand eyes are counted as five times two hundred (ஐ-இருநூற்று), and line 8 answers with இரு நூற்று in the bride's own epithet. Siva's holding of the Ganga is told without naming the river.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god by his birth and his hill: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து under paadaan (porul 2.27)

comparisons.tenor: the flood held on Siva's hair
the tears of the bride's eyes

tamil: தோள் புதிது உண்ட பரத்தை இல் சிவப்புற
அதனால், அகறல் அறியா அணி இழை நல்லார்
இகல் தலைக்கொண்டு துனிக்கும் தவறு இலர்; இத்
தள்ளாப் பொருள் இயல்பின் தண் தமிழ் ஆய்வந்திலார்
reading: The poet turns to the poets of truthful speech who expound the four Vedas and tells them the order of love: what excels is desire born of love, and within desire the bodily union of two who long alike; above the quarrel stands karpu, which holds within it the courtesan with her begging and giving, the courteous reproach, and the சுணங்கறை where the wife adorns herself and rejoices to make the courtesan who newly enjoyed his shoulders flush, words spoken in the house to trouble the husband, and the fruit of that too lies in the sulk; so women who never part are not at fault when they quarrel and sulk, and those who have not studied cool Tamil with its unshakable rule of porul will not take what this hill yields.
nuance: The poet addresses Vedic scholars as outsiders and tells them that what this hill teaches is the porul grammar of Tamil, so the god's household quarrel that follows (lines 27 to 69) is offered as a lesson in akam theory, not as scandal. The ranking is a small treatise: love, then equal union, then karpu, with the courtesan and the sulk placed inside karpu rather than against it. சுணங்கறை is a rare word whose sense we cannot fix, and the clause order of lines 16 to 22 is a reading.

thinai_evidence.note: the passage defends the wife's sulk against the courtesan, the uri of marutham

tamil: ஊழ் ஆரத்து ஓய் கரை நூக்கி, புனல் தந்த
காழ் ஆரத்து அம் புகை சுற்றிய தார் மார்பின்,
‘வாழிய, மாயா! நின் தவறு இலை; எம் போலும்
கேழ் இலார் மாண் நலம் உண்கோ, திரு உடையார்
வை எயிற்று எய்யா மகளிர் திறம் இனிப்
பெய்ய உழக்கும், மழைக் கா; மற்று ஐய!‘
கரையா வெந் நோக்கத்தான் கை சுட்டி, பெண்டின்
இகலின் இகந்தாளை, அவ் வேள் தலைக் கண்ணி
ஒருவர் மயில் ஒருவர் ஒண் மயிலோடு ஏல,
reading: As the god comes in, his chest garland wreathed in the smoke of sandal that the river carried down breaking its banks, a bright pearl chain shining on him, one wife does not bow but says, 'Long live, Maaya, the fault is not yours: would you, who rest on the soft shoulders of the fortunate, deign to enjoy the beauty of plain women like us? The rain-grove will be trampled by what the sharp-toothed girls do'; then, pointing with her hand, crying 'don't come near', she binds tight and beats with her garland for a rod the woman who outdid her in the women's quarrel, the Vel who pays tribute with his head-garland touching her fine feet, and the woman who gives him her chest saying 'don't grieve'; and one wife's peacock closes with the other's bright peacock, the two parrots babble at the meeting, and a bee of the possessed god's hill leaps onto a thick hair-knot.
nuance: 'The fault is not yours' is blame in the form of a blessing. The god who bows his garland to a woman's feet pays திறை, a conquered king's tribute, so the war god is defeated in love; in the closing line he is வெறி கொண்டான், the god of the possession rite, now the cause of a domestic fray. Who bows to whose feet is a reading: the three accusatives of lines 36 to 38 can be taken as the rival, the god and the rival again, and lines 33 and 34 are obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife's sulk at the god who comes from another woman, marutham's uri on a kurinji hill

comparisons.tenor: the garland she beats them with
the god bowing to a woman's feet

tamil: தார் தார் பிணக்குவார்; கண்ணி ஓச்சித் தடுமாறுவார்;
மார்பு அணி கொங்கை வார் மத்திகையாப் புடைப்பார்;
கயம்படு கமழ் சென்னிக் களிற்று இயல் கைம்மாறுவார்;
தேர் அணி அணி கயிறு தெரிபு வருவார்
வரி சிலை வளைய மார்பு உற வாங்குவார்
குறிஞ்சிக் குன்றவர் மறம் கெழு வள்ளி தமர்
reading: The women of the two sides join in: they tangle garland with garland, swing their chaplets and stumble, lash with the bands of their breasts as whips, hurl balls wound with garlands, and, their innocent glances changed, their thin waists swaying, take the head of the fray, shifting into the gait of a musth elephant, coming on like horses in their course, as if sorting chariot ropes, bending striped bows to the chest, setting arrow against arrow and whirling bangles like discs, as the soft peacock-gaited women and the soft-spoken flower-eyed companions of the sky-king's daughter close round the broad-chested god; some bathe in the guarded pool, some pluck strings like honey-drinking bees, some spread their tails and dance like crested peacocks, some call like cuckoos, some raise a clamour; and because Valli's kin, the fierce hill-men of the kurinji, made of it a skilful thumbai battle, cool Parankunram became fit for the god of the victorious spear.
nuance: The poem names the play-fight thumbai, the puram thinai of pitched battle, and gives it the full order of an army (elephant, horse, chariot, bow, arrow, disc) played with garlands, breastbands and balls: the war god's household quarrel is staged in war's own grammar, and the hill is said to befit him for that very reason. Lines 61 to 66 move from the fray to bathing, music and dance, perhaps the same women after the quarrel. Valli's hill kin take her side, so the co-wives' quarrel is also a quarrel of the hill against the sky.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem itself calls the co-wives' play-fight a thumbai battle

comparisons.tenor: the women's gait in the fray

tamil: கடுஞ் சூர் மா முதல் தடிந்து அறுத்த வேல்
கற்பு இணை நெறியூடு அற்பு இணைக் கிழமை
நயத் தகு மரபின் வியத் தகு குமர!
வாழ்த்தினேம் பரவுதும், தாழ்த்துத் தலை, நினை யாம்
reading: Addressing the warrior whose spear cut down fierce Sur at the root of his great mango form, the poet says that on the god's hill dancers outdo dancers, panar outdo those practised in song, the skilled the skilled and the unskilled the unskilled, and, as if at one word, a banner stands beside the cool pool that has taken in the fresh red flood, with spears and with victory flags raised high that hold the worth of valour; hailing the wondrous Kumara of a lineage worth loving, lord of the bond of love along the path of the bond of karpu, he says: we have praised you and with bowed heads worship you; may our service at your feet, which excels in our love for you, excel in its fruit and flourish day by day.
nuance: Line 81 sets the god's two unions in one phrase, the bond of karpu and the bond of love, which closes the argument of lines 12 to 26: the god who holds both is the model of the order the poet taught the Vedic scholars. The contest of like with like (lines 72 to 75) mirrors the co-wives' quarrel: on this hill rivalry itself keeps its proper pairs. Line 79 is a repaired reading and its sense is thin.

thinai_evidence.note: closing praise and prayer: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து under paadaan (porul 2.27)

title: வையை (10)
theme: Paripadal 10, the Vaigai: the flood announced by drums, the whole of Koodal going out to bathe, lovers' embraces and sulks, a tusker calming his frightened mate, love and toddy hidden from gossip, offerings and water-play, evening in the town, and the flood praised as giving like the Pandya.
source_issues: Paripadal 10: the core text has 130 lines but the source numbers its last line 131; printed line 100 stands on line 99 (flags).
Paripadal 10 line 9: flagged as a line once taken for a modern heading; it reads as verse (புனல் மண்டி ஆடல் புரிவான்) and is marked as such.
Paripadal 10 lines 28, 29, 42, 43, 44, 126, 129, 130 are not in sangamtamil.com's text; ours kept (flags).
Paripadal 10 lines 69, 88 and 108: repaired from sangamtamil.com readings (flags).
Paripadal 10 line 97: போன்ம் is written three times (போன்ம் போன்ம் போன்ம்); possibly a copying repetition.
Paripadal 10: the colophon has no thinai or thurai; the pan is பாலையாழ், a musical mode, not a thinai.

tamil: வரி அரி ஆணு முகிழ் விரி சினைய
ஆய்ந்து அளவா ஓசை அறையூஉப், பறை அறையப்
reading: When the rain has fallen on the mountain range in the evening and run on to join the sea whose bounds no one sees, easing the land's distress, the Vaigai's flood arrives, spreading its coarse sand like a many-folded coverlet, mixing tender striped mango shoots with plantain leaves, its sound beyond measure while drums are beaten to announce it.
nuance: The flood is given a herald: பறை அறைய in line 7 is the drum that tells the town the water has come, so the river enters the poem like a king entering a city. மாலை in line 1 may be 'evening' or 'the range' (the hills as a garland); the reading takes the hour.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet hails the river's coming as an event announced by drums: praise of the Vaigai (porul 2.27)

comparisons.tenor: the coarse sand the flood spreads over the bed

tamil: புனல் மண்டி ஆடல் புரிவான், சனம் மண்டி,
முத்து நீர்ச் சாந்து அடைந்த மூஉய்த் தத்தி;
புக அரும் பொங்குஉளைப் புள் இயல் மாவும்,
மிக வரினும் மீது இனிய வேழப் பிணவும்,
வகை வகை ஊழ் ஊழ் கதழ்பு மூழ்த்து ஏறி;
reading: To play in the flood the people crowd out, with fine threads tied at their feet and girdles of many strands pulled tight, carrying syringes of blood-red lac water and pearl-water paste, and they harness plumed horses swift as birds, she-elephants sweet to ride even when the water runs high, carts, mules, fine bullock carts and pole palanquins, and mount them in turn, hurrying in rows.
nuance: The preparations are for a water-fight as much as a bath: நீரெக்கி (line 12) are squirts filled with red lac water, the festival weapon that returns in the play of lines 99 to 110.

thinai_evidence.note: the crowd dresses and sets out for play in the river flood, the bathing of the watered-field land

comparisons.tenor: the rows of strands of the girdle
the lac dye in the water syringes

tamil: வதி மண வம்பு அலர் வாய் அவிழ்ந்தன்னார்
விதி கூட்டிய இய மென் நடை போல,
பதி எதிர் சென்று, பரூஉக் கரை நண்ணி
நீர் அணி காண்போர்; நிரை மாடம் ஊர்குவோர்;
பேர் அணி நிற்போர்; பெரும் பூசல் தாக்குவோர்;
மா மலி ஊர்வோர்; வயப் பிடி உந்துவோர்;
வீ மலி கான் யாற்றின் துருத்தி குறுகி,
தாம் வீழ்வார் ஆகம் தழுவுவோர்; தழுவு எதிராது,
யாமக் குறை ஊடல் இன் நசைத் தேன் நுகர்வோர்;
சேமத் திரை வீழ்த்து சென்று, அமளி சேர்குவோர்:
பூ மேம்பாடு உற்ற புனை சுரும்பின், சேம
மட நடைப் பாட்டியர்த் தப்பி, தடை இறந்து,
தாம் வேண்டும் பட்டினம் எய்திக் கரை சேரும்
யாம் வேண்டும் வையைப் புனல் எதிர்கொள் கூடல்
reading: Old and young, girls in the bud, new brides like flowers just opened, the rich, the dear ones, the half-grey and the white-haired, chaste wives, courtesans and companions all go from the town to the wide bank in a soft pace like music set to the drummers' beat, and there some watch the water, some ride the floats, some fight, ride horses or drive she-elephants, while near the flowered island some embrace the ones they love, some refuse the embrace and taste the honey of a sulk at night's end, and some, with love as the pick that breaks resistance, drop the screen and go to bed; and Koodal receives the flood we long for as women who escape their slow old guardians to meet their husbands, as men at a port receive the ship that reaches shore.
nuance: The list of bathers in line 23 sets பதிவத மாதர் and பரத்தையர் side by side, chaste wives and courtesans in one festival crowd, which the akam poems never do. The closing simile makes the whole city a lover: Koodal meets its flood as a wife meets the husband she has waited for.

thinai_evidence.note: the lovers' embrace and sulk at the river island, union in the watered land

comparisons.tenor: the crowd's measured going to the river

tamil: ஆங்க அணி நிலை மாடத்து அணி நின்ற பாங்காம்
மடப் பிடி கண்டு, வயக் கரி மால் உற்று,
செல் மனம் மால் உறுப்ப, சென்று; எழில் மாடத்துக்
கை புனை கிளர் வேங்கை காணிய வெருவுற்று,
மை புரை மடப் பிடி, மட நல்லார் விதிர்ப்புற,
செய் தொழில் கொள்ளாது, மதி செத்துச் சிதைதர;
கூம் கை மத மாக் கொடுந் தோட்டி கைந் நீவி
பருக் கோட்டு யாழ்ப் பக்கம் பாடலோடு ஆடல்
reading: A strong tusker sees a gentle she-elephant standing by an ornamented mansion, falls into longing and will not walk; she, going toward him with her heart on him, sees the tiger painted on the mansion wall, takes fright, ignores her driver and bolts while the women on her tremble, and the tusker shakes off his goad, trumpets like thunder, turns back, embraces her and twines his legs with hers, the beloved ending the beloved's fear like a pilot who knows the quarters mending with resin a ship whose sail and gear are giving way; then lovers whose fortified hearts the lute, song and dance have broken stand ashamed before the crowd, unable to choose, like two kings' armies that met and now stand joined, afraid to sound the cry of truce.
nuance: This is not iraicchi in the brief's sense: line 52 states the sense outright (சிறந்தார் நடுக்கம் சிறந்தார் களையல்) and two explicit similes follow, so the elephants are the subject and the deletion test fails. It is the akam elephant-pair image with its meaning spelled out. The fright is caused by a painted tiger, art mistaken for a beast. Lines 53 and 56 to 62 are compressed; what இதை, களிறு and பிணை name on the ship (sail and fittings) and who the shamed ones of lines 57 to 59 are is a reading.

thinai_evidence.note: the beloved's fear ended by the beloved's embrace, shown in a pair of elephants

comparisons.tenor: the women walking with the she-elephant

tamil: காமம் கனைந்து எழ, கண்ணின் களி எழ,
கள்ளின் களி எழக் காத்தாங்கு, அலர் அஞ்சி,
உள்ளம் உளை எழ, ஊக்கத்தான் உள் உள்
பரப்பி மதர் நடுக்கிப் பார் அலர் தூற்றக்
reading: As love surges and joy shows in the eyes, those who hide, fearing even the town's ruler, are like drinkers who guard their drunkenness: dreading gossip, hearts in turmoil, they suppress their high spirits while the world spreads talk, and so this flood brings toddy mixed with love that tears away the banks.
nuance: Love and toddy are joined twice, first as simile (the lover hides his joy as the drinker hides his drink) and then as the flood's own cargo (கள்ளொடு காமம் கலந்து). ஊர் மன்னும் (line 64) may be the town's king or simply 'the town' with a particle; the fear is in any case of being seen.

thinai_evidence.note: lovers who hide their union from the gossip of the crowd

comparisons.tenor: lovers who keep their love's excitement hidden
love and toddy that overflow restraint

tamil: கனல் பொருத அகிலின் ஆவி கா எழ,
நகில் முகடு மெழுகிய அளறு மடை திறந்து
திகை முழுது கமழ, முகில் அகடு கழி மதியின்
உறை கழி வள்ளத்து உறு நறவு வாக்குநர்,
அரவு செறி உவவு மதியென அங்கையில் தாங்கி,
ஏறி மகர வலயம் அணி திகழ் நுதலியர்,
மதி உண் அரமகளென, ஆம்பல் வாய் மடுப்ப;
மீப்பால் வெண் துகில் போர்க்குநர்; பூப் பால்
நத்தொடு, நள்ளி, நடை இறவு, வய வாளை,
reading: Tired from fighting the water, bathers leave their rafts; the smoke of burnt agil rises in the grove and the paste on women's breasts runs off like an opened sluice so that every quarter smells of it; some pour toddy from a cup uncovered like the moon slipping out of a cloud, and women with makara bands on their bright foreheads hold it in their palms like the full moon caught by the serpent and drink with lily mouths like celestial women drinking the moon; some wrap white silk, some twist their hair, some grind red saffron, agil and camphor into a paste red as sacrificial fire; some release snails, crabs, prawns and vaalai fish into the waves crying 'grow and flourish', and some, looking to what they lack, do good works in hope before they would ever speak the shame of asking.
nuance: Lines 85 to 88 are the rite inside the play: creatures are given back to the river with a blessing, and wishes are made by deeds instead of by asking, so that இளிவரவு, the humiliation the Kural attaches to begging, is kept out even of prayer. Several similes of lines 73 to 84 (the serpent-seized moon, the moon-drinking women, the oblation fire) are compressed and their exact tenors are a reading.

nuance: The simile turns the festival into a battle: the clear river is muddied as a war-field is trampled by elephants, and the young men's mock fight with weapons belongs to the same picture. The kandal is a seashore plant, out of place in the river scene.

reading: Like the Vazhuthi who pours gold until the outstretched hands of poets in want are full, the flood spreads its water and pours gold on the fields, and may that work never cease, says Koodal, which without strain feasts the flood that comes as a guest, while musicians and the household companions together praise it and bow.
nuance: The usual direction of Tamil praise is reversed: kings are likened to rain and river, but here the river is likened to the king, so the Pandya's giving is the fixed measure and nature is measured against it. The city treats the flood as a guest (விருந்து அயர் கூடல்). அருங் கறை in line 129 is obscure.

title: வையை (11)
theme: Paripadal 11, to the Vaigai: the flood dated by the stars, the flowers it carries to the ford, a plea that the river go gently, the town's water-sport drawn as war, the maidens' Thai bath under the brahmins' rite, a youth swept off by the current as a girl takes his heart, the bathers' prayers for lasting love, and a close that names the song a kaikkilai.
source_issues: Paripadal 11: the colophon has no thinai or thurai; the pan is பாலையாழ், a musical mode, not a thinai. The song names its own theme in line 136 (கைக்கிளைக் காம).
Paripadal 11 line 59: உருகெமு is a misprint for உருகெழு (as in line 4).
Paripadal 11 line 113: எந்று is a misprint for என்று.
Paripadal 11 lines 100 and 127: ஒர் and ஒர்மின் for ஓர் and ஓர்மின் (lost vowel length).

Paripadal 11 lines 1, 51, 64 and 137: flagged as places where a line was taken for a modern heading and dropped; the text as printed reads continuously at each, but this was not verified against another edition.
Paripadal 11 lines 32-34, 50-53 and 56-60 are not in sangamtamil.com's text; ours kept (flags). Line 47: lost vowel sign restored in படையொடும் by rule (flag).

tamil: எரி, சடை, எழில் வேழம், தலையெனக் கீழ் இருந்து,
இல்லத் துணைக்கு உப்பால் எய்த, இறை யமன்
வில்லின் கடை மகரம் மேவ, பாம்பு ஒல்லை
எதிர் வரவு மாரி இயைக என இவ் ஆற்றால்
புரை கெழு சையம் பொழி மழை தாழ,
reading: The poet fixes the hour of the flood by the sky: with the moon among the twenty-seven stars that the fire-star, the matted one and the elephant head, Venus come to the Bull, the earth's son to the Ram, Mercury joined to the Twins, the fire high at dawn, the other planets at their stations by the Bow and Capricorn, the serpent swiftly hiding the moon, and the star of the sage of Pothiyil reaching the Twins, so that rain might come to meet the blazing summer; and by this course the rain falls low on the lofty Sahya and the Vaigai's flood comes crowding down.
nuance: The song opens not with a god but with a dated sky: the river's coming is placed inside the order of stars and planets, as if the flood were a festival with its own horoscope. Which planet each name in lines 7 to 9 stands for (அந்தணன், பங்கு, இறை யமன்) is a reading, not a certainty, and the eclipse of line 9 (பாம்பு ... மதியம் மறைய) may be a fixed event or a figure.

thinai_evidence.note: the coming of the Vaigai flood told as praise of the river, under paadaan

tamil: வண்டு அறைஇய சண்பக நிரை, தண் பதம்
ஊதை அவிழ்த்த உடை இதழ் ஒள் நீலம்,
அரி மலர் மீப் போர்வை, ஆரம் தாழ் மார்பின்,
திரை நுரை மென் பொகுட்டுத் தேம் மணச் சாந்தின்
reading: The flood brings down the punnai of the hills and the surapunnai of the banks, rows of champak hummed over by bees, the house mango, the vaal veeram, the branching vengai, the wide-opened kaanthal, thondri blooming like fire and bright blue lilies opened by the wind, choking the falls of the bamboo groves and driving them on its leaping waves, so that the poet asks whether to call the great Thirumarudam ford a ford of flowers cut by the reapers, a woman's garment with flowers for its upper cloth, foam for its pearl-hung breast and fragrant paste for its sandal, or the throat of a drinker gulping toddy.
nuance: The three 'shall I call it' questions (என்கோ, lines 25 to 29) give the same ford three bodies: worked land, a dressed woman and a drunk man, so the flood is at once harvest, ornament and intoxication. ஆய் கோல் வயவர் (lines 24, 25) may be reapers or warriors; the sense of the first figure is not secure. The flowers are mostly of the hill, carried down into the town's ford.

நாளின், நாளின், நளி வரைச் சிலம்பு தொட்டு,
உலகு பயம் பகர; ஓம்பு பெரும் பக்கம்
எண் மதி நிறை, உவா இருள் மதி போல
சேண் இகந்து கல் ஊர்ந்த மாண் இழை வையை!
வயத் தணிந்து ஏகு, நின் யாணர் இறு நாள் பெற!
மா மயில் அன்னார், மறையில் புணர் மைந்தர்,
காமம் கள விட்டு, கைகொள் கற்பு உற்றென,
மல்லல் புனல் வையை! மா மலை விட்டு, இருத்தல்
reading: Like the waxing fortnight of the full moon the flood grows day by day, touches the slopes of the thick hills and spreads over the land as moonlight spreads, so that the world yields its fruit; then, as the moon's fullness wastes in the fortnight when the gods take their food from it, the flow shrinks, and who notices the days run down like the moon of the dark new-moon after its fullness? So the poet asks the jewelled Vaigai, who came from afar riding over stones, to go gently that her plenty may last its full term, and tells her that, as peacock-like women who joined young men in secret leave stealth and take up chastity, for her to leave the great mountain and go alone to a house would be a shame.
nuance: The river is spoken to as a bride: the move from களவு to கற்பு (line 42) is the passage she is making from the hill to the plain, and the poet's counsel is that she not go alone, that is, that her flood go with its full train. The word இளிவரல் (line 44) is a judgment of shame, not the meyppadu of that name, whose causes are age and illness. The run of lines 41 to 44 is compressed and its exact construction is a reading.

இடை நெறித் தாக்குற்றது ஏய்ப்ப, அடல் மதுரை
ஆற்று அணி, வெள் வாள் விதிர்ப்போர், மிளிர் குந்தம் ஏந்துவோர்,

புள் ஏர் புரவி பொலம் படைக் கைம்மாவை
வெள்ள நீர் நீத்தத்துள் ஊர்பு ஊர்பு உழக்குநரும்,
வண்ண நீர் கரந்த வட்டு விட்டு எறிவோரும்,
தெரி கோதை நல்லார் தம் கேளிர்த் திளைக்கும்
reading: As when kinsmen fall on a youth in mid-road as he carries off with his band a girl whose long wide eyes outrun their corners, the flood strikes warlike Madurai and its water is fit for play: the river's array is men brandishing white swords and lifting gleaming lances, men mounting strong bannered chariots as the drivers take the goad, men who ride bird-swift horses and gold-trapped elephants again and again through the flood, men who throw balls hiding coloured water at those who chase with poles, and men who squirt water from rough horns at those who whirl fragrant garlands, so that, when one tells the fearsome sight of the well-garlanded women sporting with their lovers, the Vaigai's waters are every day like a field of battle.
nuance: The water-sport is drawn entirely in the terms of war (swords, lances, chariots, horses, elephants, a battlefield), and the opening simile is itself an elopement broken by the girl's kin: the flood that breaks on the town is the pursuing family, and the town is the couple. Lines 54 to 57 (கழித் துரப்போரை, வட்டு, மருப்பின் நீர் எக்குவோரும்) name games whose exact form is not clear.

தார் வரை அகலத்து, அவ் ஏர் அணி நேர் இழை
ஒளி திகழ் தகை வகை செறி பொறி
பாகர் இறை வழை மது நுகர்பு, களி பரந்து,
நாகரின் நல் வள வினை வயவு ஏற நளி புணர்மார்,
காரிகை மது ஒருவரின் ஒருவர் கண்ணின் கவர்புற,
சீர் அமை பாடற் பயத்தால் கிளர் செவி தெவி,
உம்பர் உறையும் ஒளி கிளர் வான் ஊர்பு ஆடும்
reading: Men with chests broad as hills, wearing cool garlands thick with fragrant water-flowers, go with women of fine jewels and worked gold garlands; they drink the honeyed wine, the elation spreads, and the townsmen press close to embrace; each draws the other's beauty in through the eyes, ears stirred by well-made song, on boats that ride like the bright cars of those who dwell above, a custom with nothing hidden; and so, O Vaigai, your turbid summer water and its clearing are not like the rains.
nuance: The unit is one long run of attributes (lines 62 to 65 heap seven qualifiers on the women's garlands) closed by a plain address to the river. கரவா வழக்கிற்று (line 71), 'a custom that does not hide', makes the lovers' play public, the opposite of the secrecy of களவு in the earlier unit. Lines 66, 67 and 72, 73 are obscure in construction.

மா இருந் திங்கள் மறு நிறை ஆதிரை
புரி நூல் அந்தணர் பொலம் கலம் ஏற்ப,
பனிப் புலர்பு ஆடி, பரு மணல் அருவியின்
நெறி நிமிர் நுடங்கு அழல் பேணிய சிறப்பின்,
மையாடல் ஆடல் மழ புலவர் மாறு எழுந்து,
பொய் ஆடல் ஆடும் புணர்ப்பின் அவர், அவர்
தீ எரிப் பாலும் செறி தவம் முன் பற்றியோ,
தாய் அருகா நின்று தவத் தைந் நீராடுதல்?
reading: When the thundering rain clouds have gone and the cold dewy shivering season comes, after the heavy rains when the sun does not scorch, on the Aathirai of the full moon the learned brahmins begin the festival and thread-wearing brahmins receive the golden vessels; praying that the wide earth not be scorched, the maidens of fine bangles in the ambaa bath, shown the order of the rite by the elder women of the ford, bathe at the cold dawn, and as the wind blows over the sandy stream they dry their wet clothes at the leaning flame the vedic priests tend; so, O Vaigai, your offering was fitting. Then the poet asks the river: is it through hard penance done before, beside the fire, that these girls bathe in the Thai water standing near their mothers, while the young poets rise against one another in their contests?
nuance: The bath is for the land, not (as later tradition has it) for a husband: the girls' stated prayer is வெம்பாதாக, வியல் நில வரைப்பு (line 80). Brahmin priests, elder women and mothers frame the maidens' rite, so the unmarried girls' bathing is a public act under guardians. Lines 88 and 89 (மையாடல் ஆடல் மழ புலவர் மாறு எழுந்து, பொய் ஆடல்) are obscure; the contest of the young poets is a reading.

thinai_evidence.note: the river's rite and offering, praise of the river under paadaan

ஆயத்துடன் நில்லாள் ஆங்கு அவன் பின் தொடரூஉ,
தாய் அத் திறம் அறியாள், தாங்கி, ‘தனிச் சேறல்;
reading: On the bank the girls adorn one another in rivalry: one, her shoulders surpassing the bamboo, sets tender asoka shoots and a blue lily at her ears, so that it is said she has made herself four eyes; another answers with a tilaka like a forehead eye, taking the look of Kotravai; one, seeing a girl in coral bangles, puts on green lily stalks; and against one who strings a kallakaaram wreath another, as if saying 'stop!', winds neythal round a jasmine garland; then in the leaping Vaigai a youth loses hold of his float the moment he sees one of them, the strong current takes his hand, she takes his heart and the long raft is swept off, his eyes stay where she stands while the water carries him where it will, she leaves her companions to follow him, and her mother, not knowing why, holds her back crying 'don't go alone, keep with your group', as the new flood from far away comes striking down.
nuance: Three pulls in one line (கை வாங்க, நெஞ்சம் அவள் வாங்க, புணை வாங்க, lines 107, 108): the river, the girl and the float each take something from him, so the flood that carries the body is the outward form of the look that carries the heart. The mother's தனிச் சேறல் (line 112) repeats the poet's word to the river in line 44: the girl and the river are warned in the same phrase. நில்லிகா and மல்லிகா (lines 104, 105) are a pun.

thinai_evidence.note: a first look between a girl and a youth that the flood and her mother cut off before any union, the love the song itself calls kaikkilai

reading: Some say 'you are worthy, Thai water, your colour has cleared'; some 'we pray that we may win the honour of embracing lovers whose arms never leave our necks'; some 'may those we love not leave us lonely as the bee leaves a fallen flower, but be our safe keeping'; some 'never saying old man and old woman, for seven births may our rich kin last, bearing children'; and the onlookers call out: this beauty is a goddess that strikes whoever sees her, her eyes are Kaaman's treasury and army; hear the swarm of bees that will not leave though the women with oiled lily garlands drive them off, holding a tune as on a lute; hear the bright paalai melody of the bees attending their kin; see the cool thumbis dancing to the beat; see the one thumbi in burning anger that dives first at the girl who crushed the flower it loved.
nuance: The four prayers rise in scope: a clear river, a lover's embrace, a lover who will not leave, and a household that lasts seven births without growing old. The angry thumbi of lines 130 to 132 guards the flower it loves against the girl who crushed it; it could be read as a figure for the lover's jealousy, but no situation in the unit is anchored to it, so it is left as scene. The music terms of lines 126 to 129 are obscure.

title: வையை (12)
theme: Paripadal 12, to the Vaiyai: the flood coming down from the hills with their trees, the town of Madurai dressing and riding out to meet it, the music at the ford, the onlookers' gossip of a husband's straying look, his wife's garland-blows and coloured water and the flood that ends her sulk, the river muddy, clear and blood-red as the war-king's river, and the festival whose fame the world cannot hold.
source_issues: Paripadal 12: the colophon has no thinai or thurai; only the subject வையை, the poet நல்வழுதியார், the music நன்னாகனார் and the pan பாலையாழ் (a musical mode, not a thinai) are given.

Paripadal 12 lines 9, 29, 38 and 39 are flagged as lines once taken for modern headings; read by eye they are verse: line 9 opens the reported news, line 29 continues the list of riders, and lines 38-39 complete the sentence begun at the end of line 37 (அவை / எல்லாம் ... அவை / கில்லா). They are kept.

Paripadal 12 has 101 lines but the source numbers its last line 100, and its printed number 60 stands on line 59; our line numbers follow show, not the printed ones. The short line 75 (என ஆங்கு) may be the one the source did not count.
Paripadal 12 line 6: ஞாழ்லும் reads as a misprint for ஞாழலும்.
Paripadal 12 line 11: வேயு மோரும் is one word split, read வேயுமோரும் as in line 16.
Paripadal 12 line 2 கிளையொடு and line 23 வளையொடு have the vowel sign ொ restored (flags); line 2 is not confirmed by sangamtamil.com.
Paripadal 12 lines 61-64 (who swears the oaths and who calls them false) and lines 94-98 (a run of terse clauses) are hard to construe; lines 89-91 do not fix whose breast the garland is set on.

reading: Clouds lit by wind-struck lightning spread darkness over the sky and close round the soft hills without pause, the rain-washed slopes shed their flowers, and the Vaiyai comes down carrying the bright-hooded cobra, eaglewood, vazhai, gnemai, sandal and the fragrant thagaram, gnaazhal and deodar, its sweet water and wind seeming to make for the full sea.
nuance: The song opens not at Madurai but at the source: the river's load is a list of hill things (kurinji trees and a hill snake), so the flood that reaches the town in line 9 arrives as the hills' gift. The simile of line 7 gives the river a will (முன்னியது, 'aimed at'): it seems bound for the sea, though the town will claim it first.

thinai_evidence.note: the coming of the river, sung as praise of the Vaiyai: paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the Vaiyai's coming down in flood

வாச நறு நெய் ஆடி, வான் துகள்
வடி மணி நெடுந் தேர் மா முள் பாய்க்குநரும்,
reading: Hearing that the cool lovely Vaiyai has come strewing flowers and beating against Madurai's wall, the town makes ready: some put on gleaming jewels, some set gold-leaf flower ornaments, some change their eaglewood paste for smoked sandal, some dress their dark hair or bind in flowers, some put on fitting cloth and clasped bead strings, some bathe in scented oil, polish their mirrors and study their colour and glow, and chew fragrant betel; men and women in bangles, armlets, anklets and honeyed garlands, fragrant from a league off, ride gentle horses, sit on she-elephants like a host of swans, spur swift horses and tuskers and belled chariots, crowding in ever greater haste with dancing everywhere, so that the water came to be Koodal's talk and the crowd came to fill its banks; the flood rose over the banks, and the watchers' longing rose as if it had seized the flood.
nuance: Lines 11 to 22 are a catalogue built on the repeated -ஓரும் ('some ... some'), the whole town as a list of acts of dressing; the river's arrival is first a rumour (எனக் கேட்டு, line 10) and the festival is the town's answer to news. Lines 32 to 35 balance the water and the crowd in matched clauses (வந்தன்று ... வந்தன்று), and the last simile turns it round: not the flood taking the people, but their longing taking the flood.

ஒன்று அல, பலபல உடன் எழுந்தன்று; அவை
ஒத்த குழலின் ஒலி எழ முழவு இமிழ்

reading: At the front ford the voices of those standing in their finery rise together, not one but many, and no one can hear them all; of what can be heard, the flute sounds in tune, the muzhavu roars with the maththari, thadaari, thannumai and maguli drums, all measured together on the beat, none falling behind, and the young women with their bright even-wristed forearms keep the time: look at them.
nuance: The poet stages the limits of report: the crowd's words cannot all be heard (lines 37 to 39), so he picks out some (கேள்வி கேட்டன சிலசில), and the episodes that follow are offered as samples overheard at the ford. The rhythm of the drums is kept by women's hands, the festival's order made visible in the same crowd that is speaking at once.

thinai_evidence.note: the music and noise of the festival crowd at the ford: paadaan

reading: Voices in the crowd: one says, is she not ashamed, friend, the woman who said he had enjoyed the beauty of a graceless courtesan's shoulders and left her, and now rides the she-elephant in the flood with that man; another, that the man who eyes the breasts of a slender girl in the company is a leaky-minded weakling; another, that a woman who heeds neither the scratches nor the words, whose colour has changed and who has followed the man down the road, shows that restraint takes fright and leaves once love has come; another bids them look at the 'pure' one who, having eyed a woman's necklace and breasts while a goddess-like woman with a nectar look watched, is beaten by his wife with her garland, his hands tied tight with her ornament, and, seeing no fault in himself, bows and asks to be told it; when she says a woman looked at him, he pleads that he never knew the woman was one of false oaths, and to his true oaths she says 'false' and twists his words; sulking and refusing him, she flings a ball of flower-coloured water, and as if from the wound of her spear-like eyes his blood runs, his heart fails and he sinks to the ground; then, troubled and afraid of a scar on his strong chest, all her quarrel passes, and the Vaiyai's flood, as always, brings her back to her lover's lovely breast.

The coloured water of the festival game becomes, by metaphor, the blood of the wound her glance made, and the reconciliation is credited at the end not to either lover but to the river (வல்லதால், வையைப் புனல்): the sulk scene is told as praise of the Vaiyai. Who swears and who answers in lines 61 to 64 is hard to fix.

கார் அடு காலை, கலிழ் செங் குருதித்தே
reading: So it goes; with jasmine, mauval, fragrant champak, alli, kazhuneer, lotus, aambal, kullai, vakulam, kurukkaththi, paathiri, the clustered naagam, naravam and surapunnai all smelling sweet, the two banks run muddy; then, settling and clearing, the river from the great dark hill, held by dams spread over the rock beds, shows heaven's beauty in the reflection of its water; and in the morning of the rains it is red with turbid blood, the river of the king whose army kills in war.
nuance: Three states of the one river follow each other: muddy with flowers, clear enough to mirror heaven, and red as blood in the monsoon. The last is turned to the king's praise: the flood's red silt is read as the blood of his wars, so the river is named by its owner's killing (போர் அடு தானையான் யாறு). The flower list mixes plants of every landscape (jasmine of mullai, lotus and aambal of the fields, punnai of the shore), the river gathering them all.

Whose breast (ஆகம்) the garland is set on, and whether கேள் in line 91 is her lover or her companion, cannot be fixed from these lines; if it is her lover, this is a small scene of union after the quarrel of lines 45 to 74.

title: திருமால் / செவ்வேள் (13, 14)
theme: Paripadal 13 and 14: Nallezhuthiyar's hymn to Thirumal, the god as mountain, as the five senses and the elements, as the reclining one, the plough-bearer and the boar, counted down through five, four, three, two and one; and Kesavanar's hymn to Sevvel, his hill in the rains and a litany of his delights; both close by calling the god mother and asking only for more worship.

Paripadal 13 line 59: துழா அய் is printed as two words (the lengthened துழாய்); the karu form is taken as துழா.

தண் அளி கொண்ட அணங்குடை நேமி மால்!
கருவி மின் அவிர் இலங்கும் பொலம் பூண்,
உரிது அமர் துறக்கமும் உரிமை நன்கு உடைத்து.
reading: The poet hails Maal, whose flowered cloth has the beauty of the sun riding over a cloud-capped gem hill, whose garland vies in colour with a waterfall of gold and gems, whose banner bears the bird and whose discus has the cool grace of the wide moon; the discus and conch in his hands are like the two different discs that adorn the sky in their season, and his holy chest, with gold ornaments flashing like lightning and a garland shaped like a waterfall, holds by right for those who worship it the heaven that is theirs.
nuance: The whole unit is a single figure of the god as a mountain: the cloth is the sun on the peak, the garland the waterfall, the ornaments the lightning, the discus and conch the sun and moon. The last clause turns the description to its use: the chest is not only beautiful but is where worshippers' heaven lies (உரிது அமர் துறக்கமும் உரிமை நன்கு உடைத்து).

thinai_evidence.note: praise of Thirumal's form and ornaments: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து under paadaan (porul 2.27)

the discus and conch held in the god's hands

reading: Taste, sound, sight, smell and touch are you, lord of killing war, and so are the faculties that take each of them; of the five just named, the sky praised as known by one is you, the wind known by two is you, the fire known by three is you, and the water known by four is you.
nuance: The count is cumulative: each element is known through one more of the five than the one before (sky by sound, wind by sound and touch, and so on), so the list is a small theory of the elements, not a catalogue. The earth, which would be known by all five, is not named; the unit stops at water and line 22 turns with அதனால் to the worlds, so either the earth is left for the hearer to supply or the poet means the whole of what follows to stand for it.

thinai_evidence.note: the god named as the senses and the elements, praise under paadaan

tamil: மின் அவிர் சுடர் மணி ஆயிரம் விரித்த
கவை நா அருந் தலைக் காண்பின் சேக்கைத்
மறம் மிகு மலி ஒலி மாறு அடி தானையால்,
திறன் இகந்து வரூஉம் அவர் உயிர் அகற்றும்
விறல் மிகு வலி ஒலி பொலிபு அகழ் புழுதியின்,
நானிலம் துளக்கு அற முழு முதல் நாற்றிய
பொலம் புனை இதழ் அணி மணி மடற் பேர் அணி
reading: Therefore the thrice-seven worlds, the root, aram, time that passed beyond all firstness, the sky, and the wind with the fire are of your side; and you are the one who, divided, became three forms: the one wearing tulasi who lies in waking sleep on the bed of the serpent with forked tongues and a thousand spread hoods flashing with gems, in the midst of the milk sea; the one of the curved plough who ploughs into the chests of those who come against him beyond measure with a roaring army, raising dust as he digs; and the tusker with the bright shining tusk that planted the whole root so that the four lands should not shake.
nuance: The three forms are the reclining Maal, the plough-bearer and the boar who raised the earth; the poem makes the plough-bearer, elsewhere Maal's elder brother, a form of Maal himself (மூஉரு ஆகிய தலைபிரி ஒருவனை). களிறு usually means an elephant, but the tusk that props the earth points to the boar. Whose form the milk sea rivals in line 25 (தன் உரு உறழும்) is unclear: the white serpent's seems likelier than the dark god's. The syntax of lines 22 to 24 is loose, and the reading of நின் மருங்கின்று as 'at your side, from you' is not secure.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the one god who became three forms, under paadaan

tamil: படர் சிறைப் பல் நிறப் பாப்புப் பகையைக்
சேவல் ஓங்கு உயர் கொடிச் செல்வ! நல் புகழவை;
கார், மலர்ப் பூவை, கடலை, இருள், மணி,
அவை ஐந்தும் உறழும் அணி கிளர் மேனியை;
வலம்புரி, வாய்பொழி, அதிர்பு வான், முழக்குச் செல்,
அவை நான்கும் உறழும்--அருள், செறல், வயின் மொழி;
reading: The poet hails the unswerving rich one who took as banner the many-coloured, wide-winged enemy of snakes, lord of the high bird banner whom good praises name in the sweet ancient word of command; his beautiful body rivals five things, the rain cloud, the kaaya flower, the sea, darkness and the sapphire, and four things, the right-whorled conch, the pouring cloud, the rumbling sky and the roaring thunderbolt, rival his grace, his wrath and his words; the shade of his anklet lies past what is finished, what is passing and what is still budding; those who praise it are without the two deeds, and his heart holds to a single deed.
nuance: The poet counts his comparisons aloud (அவை ஐந்தும், அவை நான்கும், அவை மூன்றும்), so the unit is built as a falling series five, four, three, two, one: five dark things for the body, four sounds for grace, wrath and speech, three times surpassed by the feet, two deeds absent, one deed in his heart. Line 47 can be read either way: the praisers have no twofold karma, or the god's feet that they praise have none. How the four sounds are shared out among arul, seral and vayin mozhi is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the god's banner, body, grace and feet, under paadaan

வலம்புரி, வாய்பொழி, அதிர்பு வான், முழக்குச் செல்

tamil: அடை இறந்து அவிழ்ந்த வள் இதழ்த் தாமரை
செரு மிகு திகிரிச் செல்வ! வெல் போர்
எரி நகை இடை இடுபு இழைத்த நறுந் தார்ப்
புரி மலர்த் துழா அய் மேவல் மார்பினோய்!
முன்னும் முன்னும் யாம் செய் தவப் பயத்தால்;
reading: Feet, hands, eyes and mouth are lotuses opened past their sheath; you are great in feet, shoulders and neck, wide in chest, hips and mind, subtle in learning, knowledge and aram, ardent in sacrifice, valour and desire, of unfailing strength and red eyes that do not rage, rich lord of the war-winning discus, whose chest loves the fragrant twisted tulasi garland set with fire-bright flowers; thinking of you as our mother we have worshipped your feet, bowed many times and praised you, by the fruit of the penance we did before and before; still more and still more, this is our desire.
nuance: The last line uses காமம், the word for erotic longing, for the wish to worship: what the devotees desire is not a gift but more of this same worship, which they treat as the fruit of past penance. The god is thought of as mother (அன்னை எனநினைஇ), not father or king. The catalogue groups the body by threes and fours with a quality for each group (பெரியை, பரியை, நுண்ணியை, வெய்யை).

thinai_evidence.note: the closing prayer of a hymn to Maal, under paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the god's feet, hands, eyes and mouth

tamil: கார் மலி கதழ் பெயல் தலைஇ, ஏற்ற
நீர் மலி நிறை சுனை பூ மலர்ந்தனவே;
தண் நறுங் கடம்பின் கமழ் தாது ஊதும்
வண்ண வண்டு இமிர் குரல் பண்ணை போன்றனவே;
நாள் மலர்க் கொன்றையும் பொலந் தார் போன்றன;
வெல் இணர் வேங்கை வியல் அறைத் தாயின,
நீர் அயல் கலித்த நெரி முகைக் காந்தள்
வார் குலை அவிழ்ந்த வள் இதழ் நிரைதொறும்,
விடு கொடிப் பிறந்த மென் தகைத் தோன்றிப்
கார் மலிந்தன்று, நின் குன்று போர் மலிந்து,
reading: The heavy rain has poured, the brimming pools are in flower; the hum of the bright bees sipping the pollen of the cool kadamba is like a band of musicians; the shoulders of the women who dwell at your feet as they dance are like the bamboo on the high slopes; the full cry of the peacock with its crest like the bright vaakai flower is like the words of those who tell lovers who joined and left, 'do not delay, come'; the fresh konrai is like a golden garland; the vengai's blossoms have spread over the broad rock so that it shows the women in tears a tiger; and along the kaanthal by the water and the soft thonri on its creepers, flowers hot as coral have spread: your hill is full of the rains, you of the shining weapon who cut down Sur in battle.
nuance: The peacock simile carries the akam convention of the rains as the season the absent lover promised to return by: on the god's hill the peacock's cry is heard as the very summons 'do not delay, come', so a love situation sits inside the praise without a speaker of its own. Line 12 is hard: it may mean that the flower-strewn rock looks like a tiger to the weeping women, or that it reports a tiger to them; the sense of அழுகை மகளிர் is not fixed.

thinai_evidence.note: the god's hill in the rains, praised as his: paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the hum of the bees at the kadamba
the vengai blossoms spread on the rock

tamil: கறை இல் கார் மழை பொங்கி அன்ன
இரு பிறப்பு, இரு பெயர், ஈர நெஞ்சத்து,
தொன் முதிர் மரபின் நின் புகழினும் பலவே!
reading: The poet hails the god who delights in the fragrant smoke of naRai rising like a spotless dark rain cloud, who with six faces and twelve shoulders won and loved the fragrant-flowered Valli, who delights in the song his kin raise as they gather round him, whose glory on the day he was born made the great ones fear him, and who delights in the aram of the brahmins, twice-born, of two names, of moist heart and one name; since you are our mother, the fruit of our worshipping you again and again, close by you, let it be these same things more and more, more even than the many of your fame of ancient ripened tradition.
nuance: The four delights the litany names are offerings and worship (the smoke, the song, the brahmins' aram) with the love of Valli set among them, so the god's love-match is counted as one of the things worship gives him. The prayer asks that the fruit of worship be அவை, 'those', most naturally the same acts again, as Paripadal 13 asks. The brahmins' string in lines 27 and 28 (இரு பிறப்பு, இரு பெயர், ... ஒரு பெயர்) is a riddle of counts whose exact referents (the two names, the one name) are not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: a litany of the god's delights ending in the prayer, under paadaan

title: திருமால் / வையை (15, 16)
theme: Paripadal 15 and 16: Ilamperuvazhuthiyar's hymn to Thirumal at Maalirunkunram, best of hills, where heaven is easily won and the two brothers of different form and one deed are worshipped with kin; and Nalvazhisiyar's Vaiyai song, the flood's coming praised place by place, a feigned bar of menstruation overrun by a lover, the flowered river as the starry sky, and a closing prayer that rain and river never fail.
source_issues: Paripadal 15 and 16: the colophons have no thinai or thurai; only the subject (திருமால், வையை), the poets, the music and the pan நோதிறம் are given.

Paripadal 15 lines 19 and 35 are flagged as dropped modern headings; both read as verse in context (the elder brother's garland simile; the spread of the name Irunkunram) and are marked as verse. Line 23 had ொ restored and line 64 was repaired from sangamtamil.com (flags); line 39 is not in sangamtamil.com.

Paripadal 15 line 11, கல் அறை கடாம் கானலும், is obscure; read as the rock cleft and its falls, a pair joined like word and meaning. Lines 24 to 28 (தாம் வீழ் காமம் ... புணஎந்து அமர் நிலையே) are compressed; line 28 புணஎந்து is read as புணர்ந்து.

Paripadal 16 lines 20, 33 and 50 are flagged as dropped modern headings; all three read as verse. Line 26 had ொ restored (flag); lines 2 and 3 had யொடு restored by rule and are not confirmed by sangamtamil.com.
Paripadal 16 line 29 prints மரு(வ) with a bracketed editorial letter. Lines 40 to 45 are hard to construe; the subject of புல்ல and குழைந்து is uncertain. Line 7 திணை பிரி புதல்வர் is obscure.

tamil: தொலையா நேமி முதல், தொல் இசை அமையும்
புலவர் ஆய்பு உரைத்த புனை நெடுங் குன்றம்
நிலவரை ஆற்றி, நிறை பயன் ஒருங்கு உடன்
மலர் அகல் மார்பின் மை படி குடுமிய
குல வரை சிலவே: குல வரை சிலவினும்
எல்லாம் வேறு வேறு உருவின் ஒரு தொழில் இருவர்த்
reading: Of the hills that poets have praised, starting from the world-rim mountain that holds the earth, many exist, few among them bring the world its full fruit, fewer still are the clan mountains with clouded peaks, and best of those is this great high hill that bears the two who differ in form but share one deed, joined like the rock cleft and its falls, like word and meaning; heaven is not easy to climb unless the one of the fragrant tulasi grants it, but at Maalirunkunram it is easily won, and that right is what we praise.
nuance: The opening narrows like a sieve (பல, then சில, then குல வரை சில, then சிறந்தது) until only one hill is left. Heaven is named twice in two lines: hard to win elsewhere (அரிதின் பெறு துறக்கம்), easy here (எளிதின் பெறல் உரிமை), so the shrine is praised as a shorter road to the same end, and even that road depends on the god's grant (நல்கின் அல்லதை).

thinai_evidence.note: praise of Thirumal's hill as the best of mountains: கடவுள் வாழ்த்து under paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the two gods of different form joined in one deed
the two gods of different form joined in one deed

tamil: அரா அணர் கயந் தலைத் தம்முன் மார்பின்
மன் புனல் இள வெயில் வளாவ இருள் வளர்வென,
பொன் புனை உடுக்கையோன் புணஎந்து அமர் நிலையே
உறழ, நனை வேங்கை ஒள் இணர் மலர,
பெருங் கலி ஞாலத்துத் தொன்று இயல் புகழது
reading: The Silambaaru comes down the hill, its swaying falls roaring, as fine as the white kadamba garland on the chest of the god's elder brother whose head is hooded by the snake, and so adorns the hill whose name runs on with Solai, Maalirunkunram, a hill that sows and ripens whatever desire people long for; think, people, how the gold-clad one dwells there joined with his brother, as darkness deepens where the young sunlight mingles with the water, and hear his fragrant fame; with blue lilies open in every spring, asoka in flower on every branch around them, ripe fruit beside unripe and the vengai's bright clusters blooming, the hill has the sweet state of Maayon himself; you who cannot go to worship, look at it and bow: the name Irunkunram has spread, its fame is ancient in the clamouring world, and the god who grants desire takes away confusion from those who see it.
nuance: The hill is made to resemble the god twice: its falls are the elder brother's white garland, and its flowering takes on Maayon's own state (மாயோன் ஒத்த). Line 34 lets those who cannot make the journey worship by sight alone (கண்டு பணிமின்), so the hill visible from afar is itself an object of worship. Lines 24 to 28 are compressed and the image of light mingling with dark water may be read of the two brothers or of the hill at dusk.

comparisons.tenor: the river's falls on the hill
